When a pre-trained transformer's vocabulary is extended — adding domain-specific tokens, a new language's subwords, or task-specific sentinels — the new embedding rows must be initialized somehow before fine-tuning, but the backbone weights (attention, FFN, LayerNorm) are frozen, meaning only those new embeddings will receive gradient updates. The central question is: how does the statistical mismatch between new token embeddings and the existing embedding manifold propagate forward through frozen layers, and what does this imply for representation quality and training dynamics? Fertility mismatch enters here because a tokenizer trained on a new domain or language will segment text differently — often into longer, coarser, or finer-grained pieces than the original tokenizer — so the semantic load per token is inconsistent: one new token may need to encode meaning that was previously distributed across three original tokens, stressing the embedding capacity before any frozen attention layer even sees it. The expert worry that beginners miss is that naive initialization strategies (random Gaussian, zero-init, or copying a "nearest neighbor" embedding) do not respect the geometry of the pre-trained embedding space — specifically, the isotropy profile, the norm distribution, and the implicit clustering structure that frozen attention heads have already specialized to exploit; an out-of-distribution embedding row will produce anomalous key/query dot products in every frozen attention layer, potentially saturating softmax or creating dead attention patterns before a single gradient step is taken. A subtler concern is gradient locality: since only new embedding rows train, the error signal that would normally propagate back to adjust frozen layer weights to accommodate the new tokens cannot flow — so the new embeddings must converge to a point that is simultaneously meaningful in isolation and compatible with frozen weight geometry, a much harder optimization target than full fine-tuning provides. This is compounded when fertility mismatch is severe (e.g., adding a morphologically rich language to an English-centric model), because high-fertility new tokens carry dense semantic content that the frozen MLP and attention projections were never calibrated to decode from a single embedding vector.

The core failure mode is FFN capacity misalignment: the frozen feed-forward layers function as key-value memories (Geva et al. 2021, "Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories") whose keys were learned to respond to specific fine-grained activation patterns corresponding to low-fertility token sequences — when a single high-fertility token must now carry the semantic content previously distributed across 3–4 tokens, the resulting hidden state after self-attention falls in a region of activation space where the frozen FFN keys have low cosine similarity to any stored pattern, producing a weighted output that is effectively an interpolation of unrelated memories rather than retrieval of the correct one. This is distinct from an attention failure: the attention mechanism can still route information correctly between positions, but the FFN at each layer acts as a local transformation calibrated to the granularity of the original tokenization — a hidden state encoding "anti-inflammatory medication dosage protocol" as a single token will activate FFN keys tuned for fragments like "anti", "inflam", "matory" and retrieve semantically diluted or orthogonal value vectors.
